stem: Give each half of the passage a two- or three-word label for what it does. Which outline matches both halves?
stimulus: Historians long assumed that patterned silk weaving in the town of Vellaro began in the 1600s, when the first large workshops there appear in records. However, a silk fragment recently found in a Vellaro church has been dated to around 1450. Its woven pattern of vines and birds shows that skilled weavers were working in the town at least a century and a half before those workshops were recorded.
choices: It presents a long-held view, then describes evidence that challenges it.
It presents a long-held view, then describes evidence that supports it.
It presents a long-held view, then traces how that view first arose.
It describes a silk fragment, then explains the technique used to weave it.
explanation: Label the halves first. Sentence 1 is 'old view.' Then 'However' brings in the 1450 fragment, which shows weaving started earlier than the old view says. That second half is 'evidence against.' Choice A matches both labels. This is the move behind SAT questions that ask which choice best describes the overall structure of a text: label each chunk, find the turn, then check both halves of every choice.

B.why: You got the first half right but missed which way the turn goes. 'However' signals that the fragment goes against the old view. It doesn't support it. Read the turn word before you trust the second half of a choice.

C.why: You stopped checking after the first half. The passage never explains where the old view came from. It only says what historians assumed, then gives evidence against it. The second half describes a move the text never makes.

D.why: You latched onto the fragment, which is a detail, and skipped the passage's job. The passage never describes how the silk was woven. It mentions the pattern only as proof of the earlier date. The key structure is the old view followed by the correction.

stem: Give each half of the passage a two- or three-word label for what it does. Which outline matches both halves?
stimulus: Immunologists have long wondered whether memory T cells in the skin stay where they are or travel through the body. To find out, one research team attached a fluorescent tag to skin T cells in mice and tracked the cells for six months. The tagged cells remained in the small patch of skin where they had been marked, suggesting that these immune cells stay in place.
choices: It poses a question, then lists several possible answers to it.
It poses a question, then describes a study that answers it.
It poses a question, then argues that it cannot yet be answered.
It describes a study, then calls for more research on its results.
explanation: Sentence 1 is 'open question': do skin T cells stay put or move? Sentences 2 and 3 are 'study answers it': the team tagged the cells, tracked them, and found they stayed put. Choice B matches both labels. On the SAT, a phrase like 'have wondered whether' or 'set out to test' often starts a question-then-study structure. Spotting it is your first step on overall-structure questions.

A.why: You checked the first half and stopped. The passage gives one answer from one study. It doesn't list several possible answers. If a choice says 'several' and you can count only one, rule it out.

C.why: You got the question right but the turn wrong. The study does answer the question: the cells 'remained' in place. The passage never says the question can't be answered.

D.why: The passage does describe a study, but it ends with the finding. Nothing in it asks for more research. Also, this choice skips the question the passage opens with.

stem: Give each half of the passage a two- or three-word label for what it does. Which outline matches both halves?
stimulus: For decades, many city health departments judged their asthma programs by counting hospital visits for asthma attacks. When the count fell, a program was considered a success. However, some researchers point out that visits can drop simply because a hospital closes or because patients start going to urgent-care clinics instead. A falling count, they argue, does not by itself show that fewer people are having attacks.
choices: It describes a common measure, then proposes a better one to replace it.
It describes a common measure, then shows why that measure is accurate.
It describes a common measure, then explains a weakness in that measure.
It names two kinds of clinics, then compares how patients use each one.
explanation: The first two sentences are 'common practice': counting hospital visits. After 'However,' the passage gives 'weakness explained': visits can fall for reasons unrelated to health. Choice C matches both labels. On real SAT overall-structure questions, this setup-then-'however' pattern is very common, and the main point usually comes after the turn.

A.why: This is the classic half-read trap. The first half is right, but the researchers only point out a problem. They never suggest a new way to measure success. The second half describes a solution the passage doesn't offer.

B.why: You reversed the turn. 'However' introduces doubt about the measure. The passage argues that a falling count may not mean fewer attacks, which is the opposite of calling the measure accurate.

D.why: Hospitals and urgent-care clinics come up only as examples of why counts can drop. The passage never compares how patients use them. You built your outline around a detail instead of the passage's main moves.

stem: Give each half of the passage a two- or three-word label for what it does. Which outline matches both halves?
stimulus: A printmaking technique can outlive the purpose it was invented for. Mezzotint, developed in the 1600s, was used mainly to copy paintings, since its roughened copper plates could imitate soft shading. When photography took over that job in the 1800s, the technique nearly disappeared. Yet in the twentieth century, artists revived mezzotint to make original prints, valuing it for the deep, velvety blacks no other method produced.
choices: It states a general claim, then gives several examples that support it.
It states a general claim, then gives an example that disproves it.
It describes an early print method, then explains how photography works.
It states a general claim, then traces one example that illustrates it.
explanation: Sentence 1 has no names or dates. It states a broad rule, so its label is 'general claim.' Everything after it follows one case, mezzotint: invented to copy paintings, almost lost to photography, then revived for a new use. That's 'one example illustrates.' Choice D matches both labels. On SAT overall-structure questions, the one sentence without specifics is usually the claim, and the concrete sentences around it are the case that shows it.

A.why: You got the first half right but didn't count the examples. Mezzotint is the only technique in the passage. The second half claims several examples when there's just one.

B.why: You read 'Yet' as a turn against the claim. Mezzotint's revival for a new purpose is exactly what 'outliving its purpose' means. The example supports the claim.

C.why: Photography matters only because it replaced mezzotint for copying paintings. The passage never explains how photography works. This choice also skips the general claim the passage opens with.
